skills.title: Create your first Skill
skills.subtitle: Turn a routine into a reproducible tool
skills.whatItIs:
Caught yourself writing the same instructions to Claude every time? 'First check X, then do Y, in format Z...'. A Skill is your ready-made checklist for a recurring task: described once, Claude invokes it on its own when the task matches.

A Skill is a folder with SKILL.md and supporting materials. Turns a one-off prompt into a stable tool — consistent quality from run to run, no rewriting rules.
skills.approach: The key is the precise `description` in the frontmatter. Whether the Skill activates depends on it. 'Does an audit' — too vague. 'Use when user asks for audit of X with Y' — a working description.
outcomes: You understand when a Skill pays off and when it's overkill
You write a SKILL.md that Claude activates correctly
You use supporting files (templates, schemas)
You define anti-triggers — when the skill should NOT fire

applyIn.title: Regular audits
applyIn.description: A Skill with a fixed report template — every audit comes out in the same format, the team reads consistently.

applyIn.title: Standard task prep
applyIn.description: A 'prep ticket' Skill with a user story + AC + risks template — turns 10 minutes of work into 1 command.

applyIn.title: Reproducible analysis
applyIn.description: A Skill with a baked-in methodology — consistent analysis quality regardless of which team member ran it.

pitfalls: Making a Skill for a one-off task — there's no return on investment.
A vague description 'does X' — Claude won't understand the trigger.
Stuffing everything into SKILL.md — it balloons to an unreadable state.

exercises.question: Write down your 5 recurring tasks. For the most frequent one, draft a SKILL.md (name, description, 5–7 steps).
exercises.hint: If the task repeats fewer than 5 times a week — pick a different one.

exercises.question: Test the Skill: ask Claude a question where it SHOULD activate, and an anti-trigger question where it should NOT.
exercises.hint: Doesn't activate when it should → loosen the description. Activates when it shouldn't → add anti-triggers.

s1.title: Choose a routine to formalize
s1.why: A Skill pays off when the process repeats ≥ 5 times a week. Otherwise you'll spend more time building it than you save.
instructions: Write down 3 tasks you repeat regularly with a similar context.
For each, answer: how similar is the process? (≥80% → Skill candidate).
Choose one — the most frequent and stable. Start there.
s1.validate: One routine is chosen and you can clearly say: 'input → steps → output'.
s1.tip: A good Skill signal — you're ALREADY catching yourself copying an old prompt.
s1.example:
Candidates:
1. ✅ Regular audit of your items — every week, same process
2. ❌ 'Help with a task' — too varied, doesn't formalize
3. ✅ Preparing a standard document — several times a day, same template

I choose: preparing the standard document — most frequent.

s2.title: Launch skill-creator
s2.why: skill-creator is Anthropic's official skill that asks everything needed and formats SKILL.md correctly.
instructions: In claude.ai (Pro+) or Claude Code: ask to activate skill-creator.
If it doesn't activate automatically — write explicitly: 'Use skill anthropic-skills:skill-creator to create a new skill'.
skill-creator will ask a series of questions — answer in detail.
s2.validate: Claude asks questions following the skill-creator structure: name, goal, triggers, steps.
s2.prompt: Use skill-creator to create a Skill for preparing developer tickets. Ask me all the necessary questions one by one.

troubleshoot.skill-creator doesn't activate: You may not have access to skills. In Claude Code they're always available; in claude.ai — on paid plans.

s3.title: Define the role and description
s3.why: Description = trigger. Whether the Skill fires when needed depends on its precision.
instructions: Name: kebab-case, short and clear (e.g., dev-task-prep).
Description: explicit triggers (when to invoke) + explicit anti-triggers (when NOT to invoke).
Use the template below.
s3.validate: Description contains specific trigger phrases and anti-triggers.
s3.tip: If your description is a single generic phrase like 'helps with tasks' — the Skill will fire on everything. Be specific.
s3.example:
name: dev-task-prep

description: Use this skill when the user asks to convert an idea, bug, or
feature request into a developer-ready ticket. Triggers on phrases like
"prepare a ticket", "make a user story", "turn this into a task for
engineering", or when user pastes raw feature descriptions and wants
structured output.

DO NOT use for: code review, architecture discussions, or when user
explicitly asks for a quick informal note.

s4.title: Describe the step-by-step workflow
s4.why: Workflow is a 'recipe'. The clearer it is, the more stable the result from run to run.
instructions: Describe 5–8 steps Claude should execute.
For each step: what it does + what output it passes to the next step.
The final step — format of the output.
s4.validate: The workflow reads like a recipe: the cook (Claude) knows each step.
s4.tip: If there are > 10 steps — the Skill is too big. Split into two linked Skills.
s4.example:
## Workflow

1. **Clarify the idea**: if description is shorter than 2 lines — ask 3 clarifying questions (context, user goal, constraints).
2. **Formulate User Story**: format 'As a [role] I want [action] so that [value]'.
3. **Acceptance Criteria**: 4–7 points in Given/When/Then format.
4. **Technical notes**: what we touch / what we do NOT touch (if applicable).
5. **Edge cases**: 3–5 negative scenarios.
6. **Estimate**: XS/S/M/L/XL with a one-line justification.
7. **DoD**: 3–5 'done when…' points.

## Output format
Markdown, ready to paste into Linear/Jira.

s5.title: Add templates/ — templates for repeatability
s5.why: Templates move details out of SKILL.md and keep it short. They also guarantee a consistent format.
instructions: Create a file templates/ticket.md inside the skill folder.
Describe in it exactly the format that should appear in the output.
In SKILL.md refer to the template: 'follow the format from templates/ticket.md'.
s5.validate: The template is saved and SKILL.md references it.
s5.tip: A template is a contract. It's easier to change than to rewrite SKILL.md every time.
s5.example:
# templates/ticket.md

## User Story
As a {role}, I want {action} so that {value}.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Given {context}, When {action}, Then {outcome}
- [ ] ...

## Technical notes
**Touch:** ...
**Don't touch:** ...

## Edge cases
- ...

## Estimate: {XS|S|M|L|XL}
{Reason in one line}

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Tests pass
- [ ] Code reviewed
- [ ] ...

s6.title: Test the trigger and run it on a real task
s6.why: A Skill that doesn't activate when needed is dead, and a real test surfaces things invisible in synthetic examples. First verify the trigger, then stabilize it on real tasks.
instructions: Write Claude a natural phrase that the Skill should fire on.
Check: did it activate or not.
Then — a phrase it should NOT fire on (anti-trigger). Confirm Claude doesn't activate the Skill.
If triggers misbehave — go back to step 3 and tighten the description.
Take a real task from your backlog.
Run it through the Skill 2–3 times.
Where the result is weak — add a rule to the Workflow or an anti-trigger to the description.
After 5–10 runs the Skill stabilizes.
s6.validate: The Skill fires on all ✅ and not on ❌; it's used in real work and you're not writing the same prompt by hand.
s6.tip: The most common problem is the Skill firing too often; the fix is to add anti-triggers. Share the Skill with the team via the repository (skills/): one Skill × 5 people = 5× the return.
s6.example:
✅ Should fire: 'Help me turn this idea into a ticket for developers'
✅ Should fire: 'Make a user story with AC from this feature description'
❌ Should NOT: 'Tell me in general terms how to write user stories' (that's a learning request, not ticket prep)

skills.trigger: You notice you write the same checklist "first X, then Y, in format Z" every time.
inputs: A reference example "what good looks like"
outputs: Ready SKILL.md with metadata + assets
Skill that Claude triggers itself on matching tasks
Versioning for the team
skills.savings: ~10-15 min per recurring task + a single quality bar

claude-code.title: Install and configure Claude Code
claude-code.subtitle: A full AI agent in the terminal
claude-code.whatItIs:
You know VS Code Copilot that completes lines of code? [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] does the same, but 10× the scope: reads your whole project, edits dozens of files, runs commands, does refactors. And it lives in your terminal, not your editor.

Anthropic's CLI tool for working with Claude directly in the terminal. Uses [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]], sub-agents, [[node:mcp|MCP servers]] and [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] as project memory. Turns the terminal into a full AI-powered development environment.
claude-code.approach: Don't try to master everything at once. Install → run [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] → try one real edit → tune [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]. Most of Claude Code's power unlocks through the CLAUDE.md you write for your own project.
outcomes: Installed Claude Code and launched it in your project
Generated CLAUDE.md with /init and tuned it
Configured basic permissions for safe commands
Understand the main slash commands and modes (Plan / Fast)

applyIn.title: Code review
applyIn.description: claude in the repo → /review → a structured audit at the level of an experienced developer in minutes.

applyIn.title: Safe refactoring
applyIn.description: Plan mode → a change plan → you approve → execution. No surprises in the code.

applyIn.title: Auto-documentation
applyIn.description: Add Hooks: README and CHANGELOG update automatically whenever files change.

pitfalls: Running outside a git repo — you lose history context.
Without CLAUDE.md the model rediscovers the project every time.
Overly broad permissions (allow: [Bash(*)]) — loss of control.

exercises.question: In your real repo: run claude → /init → tune CLAUDE.md (add a 'forbidden' section with your rules).
exercises.hint: At least 3 lines in the forbidden section — this shows the result immediately.

exercises.question: Make a small edit (rename a variable) through Plan mode. Compare with doing the same in normal mode.
exercises.hint: Plan mode = 'show the plan first, I'll approve'. Very quickly becomes the default.

s1.title: Install Node.js and install Claude Code globally
s1.why: Claude Code is an npm package — without Node.js it won't run. A global install lets you call `claude` from any folder.
instructions: Check Node.js: open terminal → `node -v`.
If there's no version or it's < 18 — install a fresh Node.js. macOS: `brew install node`. Windows: download the installer from nodejs.org.
`node -v` should show 18.x or higher.
Install Claude Code: `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`.
Wait ~30 seconds, then verify: `claude --version`.
`claude --version` prints the version number without errors.
s1.validate: `node -v` shows 18.x or higher, and `claude --version` prints the version number without errors.
s1.tip: If `command not found: node` — restart the terminal after installing or check PATH. On `EACCES permission denied` (macOS/Linux) use `sudo npm install -g ...` or configure npm prefix to your own ~/.npm-global. On `EEXIST file already exists` remove the old version first: `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`.

s2.title: Launch in a repository and authenticate
s2.why: Claude Code works in the context of a folder. Authentication is once per machine.
instructions: Navigate to any project folder: `cd ~/projects/my-project`.
Run: `claude`.
On first run a browser opens for Anthropic authentication — sign in.
After that you're in an interactive Claude session.
s2.validate: The terminal shows a Claude prompt; you can type messages.
s2.tip: Works best in a git repository — Claude sees the history and diff. Outside a repo it loses half its features.

s3.title: Generate CLAUDE.md with /init
s3.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's 'personality'. Claude reads it on every launch and doesn't ask about the obvious.
instructions: In the Claude session type: `/init`.
Claude scans the project and proposes a CLAUDE.md draft.
Read it. Remove what's inaccurate, add rules and forbidden actions.
Save. The file lives in the project root.

Example CLAUDE.md content:

# CLAUDE.md

## Stack
- Next.js 14, App Router
- Tailwind CSS
- TypeScript (strict)

## Conventions
- NEVER use `any`. Only `unknown` or strict types.
- Tests — Vitest, not Jest. Files next to source: `foo.ts` + `foo.test.ts`.
- All components — functional with TypeScript.

## Forbidden
- Don't add extra UI libraries. Tailwind + our components only.
- Don't rewrite `auth/` without sign-off — there's legal compliance there.

## Entry points
- src/app/(routes)/page.tsx — main
- src/lib/api.ts — all external calls (no direct fetch outside)
s3.validate: CLAUDE.md is in the repo root, filled with rules specific to YOUR project.
s3.tip: Don't describe the obvious. 'This is a React project' — noise. 'Only functional components' — a rule.

s4.title: Run /security-review and configure your first Hook
s4.why: Slash commands give you ready-made workflows, and Hooks automate behavior you don't want to rely on Claude 'remembering'.
instructions: Make a simple code change, commit it (but don't push).
In the Claude session: `/security-review` — Claude analyzes the diff and produces a list of security findings.
Study the report — even if the code is clean you'll see what Claude can do.
Now configure a Hook: create the file `.claude/settings.json` (or open the existing one).
Add a PostToolUse:Write hook — it will run prettier after every file edit. Restart claude and make a test edit.
s4.validate: A structured security report received, and after every file edit Claude automatically runs prettier.
s4.tip: Build /security-review into a pre-merge habit for serious changes — more thorough than any junior. Hooks = 'junior's discipline': linter, tests, typecheck — all in hooks, the model won't forget. If a hook does not fire — check that settings.json is valid JSON and restart `claude`. In the command use `$CLAUDE_FILE_PATH`, don't guess the path.

s5.title: Create a custom subagent
s5.why: A subagent takes over a large task and doesn't pollute the main context. The best investment in productivity.
instructions: Create the file `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md`.
Describe the role, tools, and instructions.
In the chat ask: 'run code-reviewer on the current changes'.
Claude will invoke the subagent, which returns a structured report.

Example `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md`:

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Use when user asks to review code changes, current diff, or specific files. Output is a structured list of issues by severity.
tools: Read, Bash
---

You are a senior code reviewer. Your job:

1. Read the diff with `git diff`.
2. For each change, check: correctness, security, readability, tests.
3. Return a markdown report:
   - 🔴 Critical (blocks merge)
   - 🟡 Important (should fix)
   - 🟢 Nit (optional)
4. For each issue: file:line + what's wrong + how to fix.

Do NOT make architectural arguments — focus on the diff in front of you.
Do NOT rewrite code yourself — only point out issues.
s5.validate: The subagent activates and produces a structured report.
s5.tip: The description is again critical. The parent agent uses it to decide whether to delegate.

s6.title: Lock it in — embed Claude Code in your workflow
s6.why: Without building it into a habit, Claude Code stays a toy. The goal — it's part of your workday.
instructions: Set up 3 regular scenarios: e.g., '/security-review before PR', 'code-reviewer on big diffs', '/init on new projects'.
Document them in the team README.
After a week — calculate how much time you saved.
s6.validate: You have 3 scenarios you use by habit, without consciously thinking 'let me try Claude'.
s6.tip: Next step — MCP. Connecting Linear/Figma/DB turns Claude Code from a code assistant into a product assistant.

claude-code.trigger: Codebase grew beyond Copilot — you need an agent that sees the whole project.
inputs: Anthropic API key or Pro subscription
outputs: Installed and authorized Claude Code
Successful /init with CLAUDE.md
Working sense of permissions and tool use
claude-code.savings: ~2-4 hours on a refactor — dozens of files in one pass

mcp.title: Connect your first MCP server
mcp.subtitle: Give Claude access to external systems
mcp.whatItIs:
You know how USB-C is one cable for everything — laptop, monitor, headphones, charger? MCP is 'USB-C for AI'. One standard so Claude can connect to anything: your Linear, Notion, database, files, GitHub — without copy-paste or homemade integrations.

[[node:mcp|MCP (Model Context Protocol)]] is Anthropic's open standard. Through an MCP server, Claude sees your real tools and works directly inside them.
mcp.approach: Start with an existing server (filesystem or github), not your own. First understand the ecosystem and data formats through a working example, then design your own.
outcomes: Understand MCP architecture: server / client / transport
Connected an existing MCP server to [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]
Tell the difference between stdio and HTTP/SSE transports
Can debug 'why MCP doesn't see data'

applyIn.title: Context from a tracker
applyIn.description: MCP to a task tracker → Claude sees fresh tickets, can comment and suggest decompositions.

applyIn.title: Documentation in context
applyIn.description: MCP to Confluence/Notion → Claude answers with your internal documentation in mind.

applyIn.title: Code access
applyIn.description: MCP to GitHub → Claude sees PRs, can comment, make review observations.

pitfalls: Connecting everything — each server loads on startup.
Destructive tools without a confirm step — risky.
Storing tokens in the project settings.json (will end up in git) instead of settings.local.json.

exercises.question: Set up an MCP server for filesystem. Ask Claude to find all .md files in your documents folder and make a table of contents.
exercises.hint: Filesystem is the safest for a first MCP. Completely local.

exercises.question: Connect MCP to one external system you use (github / linear / notion). Ask a real question: 'what's happening in project X'.
exercises.hint: If nothing found — check /mcp in Claude Code: did the server start? Are tools visible?

s1.title: Understand why you need MCP
s1.why: Without MCP, Claude only sees what you paste manually. With MCP — it lives in your environment.
instructions: Write down 3 tools you use daily (Linear, Figma, DB, Slack...).
For each: 'what could Claude do if it could see this?'.
Choose ONE — the most frequent. Start there.
Example. Candidates: Linear (daily, lots of context in tickets), Figma (weekly, designs, need handoff to code), Notion (rarely) — I'll start with Linear.
s1.validate: One server chosen for connection.
s1.tip: Good sign: you catch yourself copy-pasting from this tool into a Claude chat. That's the MCP ROI signal.

s2.title: Find an existing server in the catalog
s2.why: 95% of services already have a server. Don't write your own — it's a waste of time.
instructions: Open the Anthropic MCP catalog or the official docs of your chosen service.
Find the server for your tool.
Copy the connection configuration.
No server in the catalog — search community repos or MCP-registry. As a last resort write your own, but that's advanced.
s2.validate: You have a snippet for settings/config with the url, tokens, and scope.
s2.tip: A prebuilt server saves hours — check the catalog before writing your own.

s3.title: Create an access token / API key
s3.why: The token is the security checkpoint. What MCP can read and change depends on its scope.
instructions: In the service (Linear/Figma/etc.) → Settings → API → Create token.
Grant the minimum necessary permissions. Prefer read-only; if writes are needed — a separate token.
Copy the token somewhere safe (1Password / Bitwarden). It's shown ONCE.
Not sure which scopes you need — take 'read-only on main resources' (e.g., Issues for Linear), expand later.
s3.validate: Token created, stored in the password manager, permissions are the minimum needed.
s3.tip: For the first connection — read-only. You can add write permission later, once you trust the server.

s4.title: Connect the MCP server to Claude Code or claude.ai
s4.why: Configuration is the most common source of errors. Follow the checklist.
instructions: Open `~/.config/claude-code/mcp.json` (Code) or Settings → Connectors ([[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]).
Add the server configuration block (see example).
Insert the token from your password manager (DON'T hardcode it — use ENV).
Restart Claude.
Server doesn't start — check JSON validity and that the token is set in ENV; run `npx <package>` separately, you'll see the error.
Authentication failed — token was copied with a space or has the wrong scope; create a new one and verify.
s4.validate: Claude restarted without errors; logs contain a line like `connected: linear` or similar.
s4.tip: Never hardcode the token in config — use ENV only, otherwise it ends up in git.

s5.title: Check the tools and make the first real request
s5.why: Without checking you don't know what the MCP server actually offers. And a real request shows the actual value — without it, MCP is setup for the sake of setup.
instructions: In the chat ask: 'show me what tools are available via MCP' — Claude will list tools with their parameter schemas.
Read the list, mark 2–3 tools that you definitely need.
If there are too many tools — ask 'keep only those for Issues and Comments active', less noise.
Take a typical task from your practice and send Claude the request — it will choose the right MCP tools automatically.
Evaluate: does the answer rely on fresh data from the service, not guesses.

Example requests. Linear: 'Show all P0 bugs in the current sprint, grouped by component, with a short risk assessment for each.' Figma: 'Open node [URL] and convert it to a React component in our design system style.' GitHub: 'Give me a summary of all PRs opened in the last 7 days, with authors and CI status.'
s5.validate: You received a list of tools with descriptions, and the answer to the real request contains fresh, accurate data from the service.
s5.tip: If Claude is uncertain — ask 'verify through MCP, not from memory'. Sometimes the model gets lazy and guesses.

s6.title: Security audit of the connection
s6.why: The MCP server sees what the token sees. Checking scope = insurance.
instructions: Open the token panel in the service → check what permissions it has.
If there's write permission — ask yourself: do I actually need write?
If in doubt — recreate the token with fewer permissions.
Enable 2FA in the service if not already.
s6.validate: The token has exactly the scopes you use, no more.
s6.tip: Never use one token for different servers. One service = one token. This simplifies revocation.

mcp.trigger: You want Claude to see your Linear / Notion / DB directly — no more copy-paste briefings.
inputs: List of systems to connect (Linear, Notion, GitHub, ...)
outputs: Working MCP server in your config
Claude reads live data from the connected system
Clear sense of stdio vs HTTP transport
mcp.savings: ~30 min per ticket — Claude pulls Linear/Notion context itself

agents.title: Create your first agent
agents.subtitle: Turn a routine into a delegatable function
agents.whatItIs: A sub-agent in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] is an isolated 'specialist' that the main Claude delegates to for a specific type of task. The agent has its own role, tools, and checklists. It turns a repeating process into a single command.
agents.approach: Don't create an agent 'for the future'. Create it for a specific routine you're doing manually 5+ times a week right now. The description is the most important thing: whether the agent activates depends on it. If it's generic ('does X') — it will never fire.

outcomes.0: Understand when an agent is needed and when a Skill is enough
outcomes.1: Wrote an agent spec: name / description / system prompt / workflow
outcomes.2: Described anti-patterns — where an agent does NOT help
outcomes.3: Launched the agent on a real task and measured the effect

0.title: Code review
0.description: Sub-agent with a review checklist → run before merge, get a filtered report.

1.title: Audit agent
1.description: Regular audit against fixed criteria → one trigger instead of a long prompt.

2.title: Researcher
2.description: Agent for gathering and synthesizing sources with web search → a report with links instead of manual work.

pitfalls.0: Making an agent for a task that comes up once a month — no ROI.
pitfalls.1: Vague description — the agent will never activate.
pitfalls.2: Trusting the agent alone — it doesn't replace the architectural thinking of an expert.

0.question: Choose one real routine (≥ 3 times a week). Write an agent spec: name, description (with specific triggers), system prompt, 5–7 workflow steps.
0.hint: The description should be such that reading it, you'd know exactly when to invoke it.

1.question: Run the agent on 3 different inputs. Check — it activates ONLY when it should. If not — tighten the description / add anti-triggers.
1.hint: Anti-triggers (what should NOT trigger it) matter more than positive triggers.

ag-1.title: Find a suitable routine
ag-1.why: A good agent automates a repeating process. Without a routine — no agent.

instructions.0: Write down processes you repeat 3+ times a week with a similar context.
instructions.1: For each: inputs, steps, outputs should be stable 80% of the time.
instructions.2: Choose ONE — the most frequent and stable.

ag-1.example:
Candidates:
1. ✅ Code review for PRs — daily, same steps
2. ✅ Regular audit of your materials — weekly, same steps
3. ❌ 'Help me discuss an idea' — too varied, not an agent

I choose: code-reviewer.
ag-1.validate: A specific routine is chosen with a clear 'input → steps → output'.
ag-1.tip: If the task requires creativity and context — that's your job, not the agent's. Agents are about repeatability.

ag-2.title: Describe the role and goal
ag-2.why: Without a clear role the agent will 'try to do everything'. Trying to do everything — it does everything poorly.

instructions.0: Write down: who is this agent (role), who does it serve (consumer), what does it output.
instructions.1: Limit the scope explicitly: what the agent does NOT do.
instructions.2: Use the template below.

ag-2.example:
Name: code-reviewer
Role: Senior code reviewer, focused on security and readability.
Consumer: Me — a developer, before opening a PR.
Output: Markdown report with a list of issues by severity (🔴/🟡/🟢).

NOT scope:
- Does not write code (only flags problems)
- Does not do architectural review (only the diff)
- Does not optimize performance (unless there are clear regressions)
ag-2.validate: Name + role + consumer + output + explicit NOT-scope written down.
ag-2.tip: NOT-scope protects against scope creep. Without it, the agent 'does everything' within a month — and does it poorly.

ag-3.title: Write the description (trigger)
ag-3.why: The description is the agent's most important artifact. Whether the parent agent delegates to it depends on this.

instructions.0: Describe: WHEN the agent should activate (trigger phrases / contexts).
instructions.1: Describe: WHEN it should NOT fire (anti-triggers).
instructions.2: Give 2–3 examples of explicit 'call me' / 'don't call me'.

ag-3.example:
description: Use when user asks to review code changes, current diff, a
specific PR, or files in their working tree. Triggers on phrases like
"review my changes", "check this PR", "code review", "look at the diff".

DO NOT use for: writing new code, architecture discussions, debugging
help, or when user explicitly asks for "quick check" — they want a
human glance, not a structured review.
ag-3.validate: Description contains specific triggers and explicit anti-triggers with examples.
ag-3.tip: The description is the most common failure point of an agent. Test it on 5+ real requests.

ag-4.title: Describe the step-by-step workflow
ag-4.why: Workflow is like training for the agent. Without it, every run is a lottery.

instructions.0: Write steps as a numbered list.
instructions.1: Each step — a concrete action + what gets passed to the next.
instructions.2: The final step — output format for the parent agent.

ag-4.example:
## Workflow

1. Read `git diff` of current changes (or specified PR).
2. For each file in diff:
   a. Check security: input validation, secrets, injection.
   b. Check correctness: edge cases, off-by-one, null handling.
   c. Check readability: naming, complexity, dead code.
3. Group findings by severity:
   - 🔴 Critical (blocks merge)
   - 🟡 Important (should fix)
   - 🟢 Nit (optional)
4. Return markdown report:
   - Top: 1-line summary (status: clean / yellow / red)
   - Per-issue: file:line + what's wrong + how to fix.
5. NEVER rewrite code — only point out issues.
ag-4.validate: The workflow reads like a recipe: it's clear what the agent does at each step.
ag-4.tip: If there are > 8 steps — the agent is too big. Split it.

ag-5.title: Create the subagent in Claude Code
ag-5.why: The agent file lives in `.claude/agents/<name>.md`. This is simpler than it sounds.

instructions.0: In the project root: `mkdir -p .claude/agents`.
instructions.1: Create the file `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md` with frontmatter (see example).
instructions.2: Restart `claude`.
instructions.3: In the chat ask: 'run code-reviewer on the current changes'.

ag-5.example:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Use when user asks to review code changes... [full description]
tools: Read, Bash
---

You are a senior code reviewer. Your job is to review code changes...

[full workflow from step 4]
ag-5.validate: The agent activates on the trigger and produces a structured report.

troubleshoot.Agent doesn't activate: Check the description — is it clear to Claude, not just to you? Tighten the triggers.
troubleshoot.Agent runs but output is wrong: Agentti toimii mutta tulos ei vastaa odotuksia
troubleshoot.Agent works but output is wrong: Tighten the workflow — especially the last step about the output format.

ag-6.title: Test and iterate on 5 real tasks
ag-6.why: Without testing the agent is a hypothesis. Real runs surface weak spots.

instructions.0: Run the agent 5 times on different real tasks.
instructions.1: Each time: what worked well, what didn't.
instructions.2: Weak spots — add rules to the workflow or anti-triggers to the description.

ag-6.validate: You have a minimum of 5 real runs; improvements are recorded in the agent file.
ag-6.tip: The best agents are born through iteration, not from 'a brilliant first draft'. Don't worry about perfection.

agents.trigger: Single Claude Code "forgets" the specifics of certain task types — you need dedicated executors for review, tests, migrations.
inputs: Task type to delegate (review, tests, refactor)
Checklist of "what a good result looks like"
Tools the agent needs access to
outputs: Ready sub-agent with role and tools
Command/trigger to invoke from main Claude
Context isolation between tasks
agents.savings: ~40% time on recurring engineering task types

subagents.title: Subagents in Claude Code
subagents.subtitle: Parallel agents — Explore, Plan, your own custom ones
subagents.whatItIs: A subagent is an isolated executor inside [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: its own context, its own tools, its own output. This is NOT a Skill (Skill = knowledge-of-how-to-do; Subagent = who-does-it). After this workshop the confusion disappears.
subagents.approach: First use the built-in subagents (Explore, Plan) on a real task — to understand what 'context isolation' means. Only then create your own. Without this order your own will be an 'under-Skill'.

outcomes.0: Run Explore to search a large repo without bloating the context
outcomes.2: Create your own custom subagent for a team routine task
outcomes.3: Know when a subagent beats a Skill (and vice versa)

0.title: Search through a large repo
0.description: Run Explore — it returns findings; your main context stays clean.

1.title: Dangerous edits
1.description: A planned refactor of 20+ files — Plan builds a plan, you review it, then apply.

2.title: Team
2.description: Your own code-reviewer, security-auditor — set up once, the whole team uses it consistently.

pitfalls.0: Using a subagent for a simple task (read 2 files) — overkill, you lose speed.
pitfalls.1: Creating your own subagent without a clear trigger in the description — it will never activate.
pitfalls.2: Giving a subagent a prompt like 'continue my reasoning' — it doesn't see your history; it needs a complete brief.
pitfalls.3: Making a subagent for 'parallelism' where tasks depend on each other — you'll get conflicting results.

0.question: Run Explore on your work repo: 'Find all places where deprecated API X is used'. Compare the time with a manual grep.
0.hint: Explore should return a structured list — not 'here are a few places', but a complete one.

1.question: Create your own subagent for a recurring task (code review / changelog / dependency audit). Run it on a real branch.
1.hint: Description = trigger. 'Use when user asks for X'. Not 'does X'.

2.question: Find a task you used to do with a Skill. Reformulate it as a subagent. Measure — where is the gain, where is the loss.
2.hint: Subagent wins on long searches; Skill wins on short reproducible procedures.

sa-1.title: Launch Claude Code in the repo
sa-1.why: Subagents are only in Claude Code, not in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]. You need an install + a project.

instructions.0: Open the terminal in the repo: cd ~/projects/your-repo
instructions.1: Run: claude
instructions.2: If first time — go through /init for CLAUDE.md.

sa-1.validate: You see the Claude Code prompt in the terminal. Session is active.

troubleshoot.Starts but no files: You're not in a git repository. Navigate to a real project.

sa-2.title: View the available subagents
sa-2.why: First — reconnaissance. What comes out of the box.

instructions.0: In the chat type: /agents
instructions.1: Read the list: Explore (search), Plan (planning), general-purpose.
instructions.2: Notice: each has a description and tools.

sa-2.validate: You have a list of 3+ subagents with descriptions.
sa-2.tip: If plugins are installed — subagents are added. That's normal.

sa-3.title: Run Explore on a real task
sa-3.why: This is the key moment — you'll understand what 'context isolation' means.

instructions.0: Phrase the task: 'Where is deprecated X used?' or 'Find all TODOs about Y'.
instructions.1: Ask: 'Run the Explore agent for searching ...' — Claude delegates itself.
instructions.2: Wait for the result — it comes as a summary, not a raw search log.
instructions.3: Check: your main context didn't inflate with files — only findings are there.

sa-3.prompt: Use the Explore agent: find all places in the repo where deprecated X is imported, and return the list with file:line.
sa-3.validate: You get a clean list 'file:line — what was found' in the main chat, without raw grep output.
sa-3.tip: If the task requires reading 5+ files — that's unambiguously Explore. If 1–2 — regular Read is faster.

sa-4.title: Run Plan before a dangerous change
sa-4.why: Plan is 'think before you act', without editing files.

instructions.0: Phrase the task: 'Rewrite all handlers of X in the style of Y'.
instructions.1: Ask: 'First run the Plan agent' — Claude returns a plan as a list of changes.
instructions.2: Read the plan critically. Find risks / omissions.
instructions.3: Approve the plan or go back to refine — then run the implementation.

sa-4.prompt: Run the Plan agent for refactoring <specific location>. I want to see the list of files, changes, and potential regressions before any edits.
sa-4.validate: You have a plan with specific file:line entries and change descriptions, WITHOUT applied changes.
sa-4.tip: Plan + manual plan review = 5× fewer 'oops' on large changes. Especially valuable on legacy.

sa-5.title: Create your own custom subagent
sa-5.why: Your own turns a regular task into a button.

instructions.0: In the chat: /agents → create new.
instructions.1: Name: e.g., security-reviewer.
instructions.2: Description: 'Use when user asks to review security of changes / PR / branch' (trigger!).
instructions.3: Steps: 1) read git diff, 2) check OWASP top-10, 3) output as a severity-ranked list.

sa-5.validate: The new agent is visible in /agents. The config is in .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md.
sa-5.tip: Description is MORE IMPORTANT than the name. Without a clear trigger the agent will never activate.

troubleshoot.Agent doesn't start on 'do a security re: Description is too generic or conflicts with another agent. Make it unique.
troubleshoot.Starts on irrelevant requests: Description is too broad. Add negative triggers: 'Use ONLY when ...'.

sa-6.title: Understand the Skill vs Subagent difference
sa-6.why: The final lock-in. Without it the confusion will return in a week.

instructions.0: Take 3 of your recurring tasks.
instructions.1: For each answer: is context isolation needed? Are custom tools needed? Is the task long?
instructions.2: All 'yes' → subagent. All 'no' → Skill. Mixed → think more.
instructions.3: Record the choice in a table: Task → Skill | Subagent | Hybrid.

sa-6.validate: You have 3 tasks with a justified tool choice. You can explain the choice in words.
sa-6.tip: Hybrid is also possible: a Skill invokes a Subagent for the heavy part — best of both worlds.

subagents.trigger: You're confused: how is a Skill different from a Subagent — and when to use which.
outputs: Working subagent with isolated context
Clear separation Skill (how to do) vs Subagent (who does)
Invocation command and result check

tool-use.title: Tool use: give Claude hands
tool-use.subtitle: Function calling — the foundation of integrations, agents and MCP
tool-use.whatItIs: [[node:cap-tools|Tool use]] (function calling) is the mechanism through which Claude calls your functions via a JSON schema. It's the basis of MCP, custom agents, and any integrations. After this workshop you understand the architecture from the inside, not as 'magic'.
tool-use.approach: Without good tool descriptions the agent will constantly make mistakes. First learn to write descriptions, then design tool sets. The actual call code is secondary — the SDK writes it.

outcomes.0: Understand the tool use flow: schema → tool selection → call → result → answer
outcomes.1: Describe a tool so Claude picks the right one 95% of the time
outcomes.2: Know when tool use beats MCP and when it's the reverse
outcomes.3: Competently design a tool set for your agent

0.title: Your own agent
0.description: Any custom agent = a system of tools. Without understanding tool use you can't build an agent.

1.title: Product integration
1.description: Claude in your app calling functions from your backend — that's tool use.

2.title: MCP architecture
2.description: An MCP server = just tools on a standard protocol. Understand tool use, you understand MCP.

pitfalls.0: Providing tools without a clear description of effects — Claude will call a destructive one with the wrong arguments.
pitfalls.1: Making a 'universal' tool with 10 parameters instead of 3 narrow ones — Claude gets confused.
pitfalls.2: Not separating read and write tools — the model mixes queries and changes.
pitfalls.3: Relying on 'the model will figure out' the parameter types — describe JSON Schema strictly.

0.question: Take a task from work (e.g., 'respond to support tickets'). Design 3–5 tools for an agent: names, parameters, effects.
0.hint: Separate read (get_ticket, list_recent) and write (reply, escalate). Each — narrow.

1.question: Take one tool from your project and write 2 versions of the description: bad (1 phrase) and good (what, when, what NOT to do). Compare Claude's choices.
1.hint: Good description = when to apply + when not to apply + example arguments.

2.question: Find a process in your work where you currently use free chat. Design how it would look through tool use.
2.hint: If the task = 'find and do' — that's an ideal tool use candidate.

tu-1.title: Understand tool use in plain terms
tu-1.why: Without an interaction model the next steps are someone else's kitchen.

instructions.0: Read the flow schema: User → Claude → Claude picks a tool → your system executes → result → Claude forms the answer.
instructions.1: Notice: Claude does NOT execute code. It only decides 'which tool to call and with what arguments'.
instructions.2: Execution is on your side (SDK / MCP-server / your backend).

tu-1.validate: You can explain in 30 seconds: who does what in the tool use flow.
tu-1.tip: This is exactly the same pattern as MCP — it's a standardized transport between Claude and tools.

tu-2.title: Read the minimal JSON tool schema
tu-2.why: This is the format Claude sees. Mastering it is mandatory.

instructions.0: Open the example: name + description + input_schema (JSON Schema).
instructions.1: Notice: input_schema describes parameters via type, description, enum, required.
instructions.2: Description is the most important part. Claude reads it to decide 'apply or not'.
instructions.3: Example: name: "get_weather", description: "Get current weather for a city. Use ONLY when user asks about current weather, not forecasts.", input_schema: { city: { type: "string" } }.

tu-2.validate: You can write a schema from scratch for a tool 'send email' — name, description, parameters.
tu-2.tip: Anthropic SDK / MCP / [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — all use the same schema. Learn once — apply everywhere.

tu-3.title: Write a good description
tu-3.why: The most common reason 'the agent doesn't work' — a bad description.

instructions.0: Template: WHAT it does (1 phrase) → WHEN to apply (trigger) → WHEN NOT to apply (anti-trigger) → EXAMPLE arguments.
instructions.1: Take your tool from exercise 2. Write the description using the template.
instructions.2: Test: give 3 different user requests — Claude should correctly decide whether to use the tool.

tu-3.prompt: description: "Send transactional email to a user (e.g. order confirmation, password reset). Use when user explicitly asks to notify a person. Do NOT use for marketing emails — those go through marketing_send. Example args: {to: \"user@x.com\", template: \"order-confirmed\", vars: {order_id: \"42\"}}"
tu-3.validate: Description contains when to apply + anti-trigger + example.
tu-3.tip: One paragraph of description often = the difference between 60% accuracy and 95%. Don't skimp.

tu-4.title: Design a narrow tool set
tu-4.why: Narrow tools = reliable agent. Broad = confusion.

instructions.0: Take the task from exercise 1. Split into read / write tools.
instructions.1: Each tool — one goal, no more than 3–5 parameters.
instructions.2: Dangerous actions (write / delete) — separate tools with an explicit confirm flag.
instructions.3: No more than 10 tools per agent. If more — split into two agents.

tu-4.validate: You have 3–7 tools, each narrow, read and write separated, dangerous ones separate.
tu-4.tip: Good sign: you can say about each tool 'when I would use it'. If you struggle — it's either redundant or poorly described.

troubleshoot.Got 15 tools: Some are redundant. Merge similar ones (if parameters align) or split the agent in two.
troubleshoot.One tool with 8 parameters: Split into 2–3 narrow ones — Claude will choose more precisely.

tu-5.title: Decide: tool use vs MCP
tu-5.why: When to write it yourself, when to use MCP.

instructions.0: Direct tool use = when tools are specific to your product, nobody else needs them.
instructions.1: MCP = when tools can be useful to multiple clients / reusable / standardization is needed.
instructions.2: Compare: is your task reusable? If yes — MCP. If unique — regular tool use.

tu-5.validate: You understand when you build an MCP server, when you just add tools for your own agent.
tu-5.tip: Company-internal CRM = tool use (nobody outside the company uses it). Postgres wrapper = MCP (universally useful).

tu-6.title: Apply to your own task
tu-6.why: Without applying this — it's all theory.

instructions.0: Take one process from work that you repeat >5 times a week.
instructions.1: Describe it as 2–3 tools (or MCP server) on paper / in Notion.
instructions.2: Don't write code — write a spec: name, description, params.

tu-6.validate: You have a specification for a real process. Ready to hand off to a developer / implement yourself.
tu-6.tip: A specification is more valuable than 'I tried to code it' — without one the code will be rewritten 3 times.

tool-use.trigger: You need Claude to call your functions / API — not just produce text.
inputs: Description of the function to call
outputs: Working tool_use loop with JSON schema
Understanding of ToolResult and error handling
Foundation for MCP / agents / integrations
tool-use.savings: ~80% integration time vs hand-parsing text responses

hooks.title: Hooks: automating discipline
hooks.subtitle: Guaranteed actions on events — no more 'I hope it won't forget'
hooks.whatItIs: Hooks are shell commands that [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] executes on events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, etc.). They run AT THE HARNESS LEVEL, not the model level. So they're reliable: the model cannot 'forget' a hook.
hooks.approach: Hooks are code, not text. First understand events and environment variables, then write your first hook on a safe action (file formatting). Only then — on sensitive ones (deny on rm -rf).

outcomes.0: Know all the key events (Pre/Post ToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit)
outcomes.1: Set up 2–3 working hooks: auto-format, guard on dangerous commands, post-edit checks
outcomes.2: Understand the difference: hook vs slash-command vs subagent
outcomes.3: Can share hooks with the team via settings.json in git

0.title: Code quality
0.description: PostToolUse:Write → prettier / linter. Guaranteed format on every edit.

1.title: Security
1.description: PreToolUse:Bash → block dangerous commands (rm -rf, git push --force) before execution.

2.title: Metrics / observability
2.description: Stop → log the session to jsonl. See what Claude did and how many tokens it spent.

pitfalls.0: A heavy shell script in a hook — slows every Claude action. A hook must be fast (<500ms).
pitfalls.1: A hook that edits the same file — can get into an infinite loop with the model. Use PostToolUse:Write carefully.
pitfalls.2: Putting hooks with secrets in the shared settings.json — they end up in git. Sensitive ones go in settings.local.json.
pitfalls.3: Using a hook instead of a subagent for long tasks — a hook blocks. Long tasks → subagent.

0.question: Find a 'after every edit of X — do Y' task in your workflow. Implement it as a PostToolUse hook.
0.hint: Classics: prettier after Write, npm test after Edit on a test file, git status after Bash.

1.question: Find a dangerous command you don't trust Claude with. Make a PreToolUse hook that blocks it.
1.hint: Template: check $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND via grep -E for the pattern → exit 1 on match.

2.question: Make a Stop hook that logs the session end to .claude/logs/session.jsonl. Use for analytics on 'what I worked on'.

hk-1.title: Understand the event model
hk-1.why: Hooks are tied to events. Know the events — know the possibilities.

instructions.0: Key ones: PreToolUse (before a tool call — can cancel), PostToolUse (after — can react).
instructions.1: Useful: Stop (session end), UserPromptSubmit (new user prompt).
instructions.2: Each event provides environment variables: $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH, $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND, $CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME.

hk-1.validate: You can name 3 events and for each — a typical use scenario.
hk-1.tip: Pre vs Post — a common source of confusion. Pre = before, you can block. Post = after, you can react.

hk-2.title: Open settings.json and find the hooks section

instructions.0: Open .claude/settings.json in the repo. If it doesn't exist — create it.
instructions.1: Find or add the section: "hooks": { ... }.
instructions.2: Under each event — an array of commands: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "..."}].

hk-2.validate: You have valid JSON with an empty hooks block.
hk-2.tip: Hooks in settings.json go into git. In settings.local.json — local only. Choose consciously.

hk-3.title: Write your first hook — auto-format

instructions.0: Add: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "npx prettier --write $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH 2>/dev/null || true"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude Code to pick up the settings.
instructions.2: Ask Claude to edit a file. After the Write — you'll see that prettier ran.
instructions.3: || true at the end — so the hook doesn't fail if the file isn't supported by prettier.

hk-3.validate: After any Claude edit — the file is automatically formatted.
hk-3.tip: The same template works for biome, eslint --fix, ruff format — any formatters.

troubleshoot.Hook doesn't fire: Check: did you restart Claude? The filename must match the prettier pattern.
troubleshoot.Claude hangs after Write: The hook is too slow. Add a timeout or move to background.

hk-4.title: Protect yourself from dangerous commands with a PreToolUse hook
hk-4.why: A real guard. Especially important if you've allowed Bash in permissions.

instructions.0: Add: "PreToolUse:Bash": [{"command": "echo \"$CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND\" | grep -qE \"rm -rf|git push --force|git reset --hard\" && exit 1 || exit 0"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude. Ask Claude to run rm -rf temp/.
instructions.2: The hook should block — Claude gets an error and doesn't run the command.

hk-4.validate: The dangerous command is blocked before execution; a safe command passes.
hk-4.tip: This is deny-by-pattern, complementing permissions.deny. Useful when permissions are too broad.

hk-5.title: Log the session via a Stop hook

instructions.0: Add: "Stop": [{"command": "echo \"$(date +%s),$CLAUDE_SESSION_ID,$CLAUDE_TOTAL_TOKENS\" >> .claude/logs/session.csv"}].
instructions.1: mkdir -p .claude/logs.
instructions.2: Work with Claude. Close the session.

hk-5.validate: Sessions are logged with timestamp + tokens.
hk-5.tip: Over the long run, these stats will show which tasks are expensive and which are cheap. Useful for optimization.

hk-6.title: Decide: hook vs slash vs subagent

instructions.0: Hook — on an event, synchronous, fast (<500ms), no decision logic.
instructions.1: Slash command — on a user trigger, can be long-running.
instructions.2: Subagent — a parallel task with context isolation.
instructions.3: Take 3 of your needs → choose a tool for each.

hk-6.validate: You can justify the choice for 3 tasks — why specifically hook / slash / subagent.
hk-6.tip: Hooks are especially valuable for guaranteed actions — the model might 'forget', a hook won't.

hooks.trigger: Claude Code sometimes "forgets" to run tests/lint before a commit — you need hard discipline.
inputs: List of events to intercept (PreToolUse, Stop, ...)
outputs: Working hooks config in settings.json
Automatic lint/test/format on the right events
Guarantee the model can't "forget"
hooks.savings: ~20-30 min/day on manual checks + zero "forgotten" tests

first-project.title: Create your first project with Claude
first-project.subtitle: From an empty computer to Claude Code running
first-project.whatItIs: An end-to-end tutorial for the absolute beginner: install Node.js, open the terminal, create a folder, install [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], run the first [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] and send the first real prompt. No assumption that "you already know cd".
first-project.approach: The tutorial branches at step 1: [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] (no terminal, you finish at step 2) or Claude Code (everything through step 6). Pick by what matters: a quick start without installs, or full control over the project files.
outcomes: Understand the difference between a claude.ai Project and a local folder
Installed Node.js and can check the version
Opened the terminal and don't fear it
Created your first working folder (two ways)
Installed Claude Code and completed authentication
Generated [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] and sent your first real prompt

applyIn.title: First day with Claude
applyIn.description: Replaces "I read the docs and nothing works" with "in 30 minutes I'm already doing things".

applyIn.title: Onboarding a coworker
applyIn.description: Share the link — and a colleague reaches the same starting state as you in half an hour.

applyIn.title: Clean install
applyIn.description: Got a new Mac or switched to Windows — run the tutorial and rebuild your work environment.

pitfalls: Skipping step 1 (choosing the path) and rushing into the terminal — only to realize a claude.ai Project would have been enough.
Creating a folder with spaces or non-ASCII in the name — then cd complains and you don't know why.
Installing an old Node.js (<18) — Claude Code will complain "engine not supported".
Skipping /init — Claude re-discovers the project every time.

exercises.question: Walk the tutorial to the end along the path you chose at step 1. Time yourself.
exercises.hint: Path A (claude.ai) — 5–10 min. Path B (Claude Code) — 25–35 min.

exercises.question: After finishing — create a second folder for a second project and verify that Claude Code picks up a different CLAUDE.md correctly.
exercises.hint: This checks you understood isolation: one project = one folder = its own context.

s1.title: Choose your path: claude.ai or Claude Code
s1.why: These are two different ways to work with Claude, both valid. Better to choose now than redo it an hour later.
instructions: claude.ai (path A): browser chat, Projects, Artifacts. No terminal. No install. Enough for most tasks: writing, analysis, discussion.
Claude Code (path B): a CLI tool that works with your local files, uses git and MCP. Needs a terminal and Node.js. For development and automation.
Rule of thumb: if your task is "discuss a document" — path A is enough. If it's "edit code in a repo" — path B.
Pick a path and commit: A → go to step 2 and finish. B → go to step 3 and the rest of the tutorial.
s1.validate: You can explain to yourself in one sentence why you picked this path.
s1.tip: Unsure — start with A. Moving to B later is no harder than now.

s2.title: Path A — create a Project in claude.ai
s2.why: A Project is your persistent workspace in claude.ai with its own instructions and knowledge base. This is the final step of the short path.
instructions: Open claude.ai → sign in (Free is enough to start, Pro is needed for Projects).
In the left sidebar find "Projects" → "+ New project".
Name: what you do + for what (e.g., "Regular report audit").
Description: 1–2 lines — what this project is for and what result you expect.
Upload 1–3 files into Project knowledge (if you have any). That's enough to start.

Done. Open the first chat in the Project and send a real prompt. Example prompt: "Using the uploaded files from Project knowledge, do the first analysis for the input: [URL / document / description]. Format — top-5 observations by priority."
If you want to continue along path B later — go to step 3. The knowledge won't be lost.
If there's no Projects section: it's a Pro feature, the Free plan hides it — either upgrade to Pro or work in regular chats without a Project.
If you don't see "New project": you may have a free Team tier — check your subscription in the top-right.
s2.validate: You have a Project with at least one real chat, and Claude's answer is concrete and references the uploaded files.
s2.tip: If you want to continue along path B later — go to step 3. The knowledge won't be lost.

s3.title: Path B — install Node.js and open the terminal
s3.why: Node.js is required to run npm packages, including Claude Code — without it nothing will install. The terminal is the workspace for Claude Code, and it's worth getting over the fear of it.
instructions: Install Node.js, macOS (recommended): open Terminal.app (Cmd+Space → "Terminal" → Enter) and run `brew install node`. If brew isn't installed — install it first from brew.sh.
Install Node.js, macOS (alternative): download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .pkg → follow the steps.
Install Node.js, Windows: download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .msi → tick "Add to PATH" → restart PowerShell.

Verify Node.js: in the terminal run `node -v`. It should print a version like v20.11.0 or newer (≥ 18). `npm -v` should also work. Version 20 or 22 LTS is optimal; 14 or 16 is old and may have issues.

If `command not found: node` — the terminal doesn't see the install: close and reopen it; on Windows make sure you ticked "Add to PATH". If `command not found: brew (mac)` — open brew.sh, copy the install command, run it in the terminal (≈5 minutes).
Open the terminal, macOS: Cmd+Space → "Terminal" → Enter. A black (or white) window with a cursor opens. Windows: Start menu → "PowerShell" or "Windows Terminal" → Enter.
Figure out where you are: run `pwd` (mac) or `pwd` / `echo %cd%` (Windows) → press Enter. It shows the current folder — usually your home: /Users/name (mac) or C:\Users\name (Windows). That's normal.
s3.validate: `node -v` prints version ≥ 18, `npm -v` works; the terminal is open and `pwd` prints the path to your home folder.
s3.tip: The "black screen" does nothing scary on its own. Only specific commands (rm -rf and similar) are dangerous, and you won't type them in this tutorial.

s4.title: Create a working folder and enter it
s4.why: A folder is the "home" of your project — without one, files pile up wherever. And Claude Code operates in the folder where you launched it: if you're not in the right one, Claude will see the wrong files.
instructions: Decide where all your projects will live. I recommend `~/projects/` in home.

Create the folder: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — creates the folder (and the parent `projects/` if it didn't exist). Alternative via Finder/Explorer: open home → create a `projects` folder → inside it another one `my-first-claude-project`.
Name — ASCII only, no spaces. Use hyphens or underscores instead of spaces.
Verify it was created: `ls ~/projects/` (mac) or `dir %USERPROFILE%\projects\` (Windows) — you'll see `my-first-claude-project` in the list.
Enter the folder: `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project`. Check: `pwd` → should print /Users/.../projects/my-first-claude-project.

Check what's inside: `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows). The folder is empty — that's normal for a new project. Memorize `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — you'll use it every time you start working.

If `permission denied` — you're creating a folder where you don't have rights: ~/ (home) is always yours, don't create folders in /Applications or /System. If `mkdir: -p: command not found` — you're on Windows in cmd.exe (old): switch to PowerShell or use `mkdir my-first-claude-project` without `-p`.
s4.validate: The folder exists, `pwd` prints the path to the new folder — you're in it.
s4.tip: `cd ..` — go up one level. `cd ~` — return home. The project name is easy to change later — it's just a folder; the key things are ASCII and no spaces.

s5.title: Install Claude Code and complete authentication
s5.why: Claude Code is Claude's "hands" in your terminal; after install the `claude` command is available everywhere. First launch is short: you authenticate once via the browser, after that Claude Code remembers you.
instructions: Install Claude Code (any folder): `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Wait 30–60 seconds — npm will download and install the package globally.
Verify the install: `claude --version` → it should print the version number with no errors.

If you get EACCES — on mac/Linux run with sudo: `sudo npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, or configure npm prefix into your own folder (~/.npm-global, google "npm permission EACCES"). If EEXIST — an old version is installed: `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then install again.
Make sure you're in your working folder: `pwd` → my-first-claude-project. Run: `claude`.
A browser opens with Anthropic auth → sign in with the same account as in claude.ai. Return to the terminal — you'll see Claude Code's interactive prompt, you can type messages.
If the browser doesn't open — copy the URL from the terminal manually and open it in the browser.
s5.validate: `claude --version` works; the terminal shows Claude Code's input field and the session is active.
s5.tip: If you accidentally closed the session — just run `claude` again from the same folder. The session's context isn't preserved, but [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] (if you have one) is picked up on the next launch.

s6.title: Create CLAUDE.md via /init and send your first real prompt
s6.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's "character": Claude reads it on every launch so it doesn't ask the same questions. And without a real prompt all of this is just an exercise — the first prompt is what the whole tutorial was for.
instructions: In the Claude session run: `/init`. Claude scans the folder (it's empty right now — that's fine) and suggests a CLAUDE.md draft.
Read the draft. Remove what doesn't fit. Add rules — e.g., "I'm not a developer, explain in plain words", or "This project is about regular report audits".
Save the file (Ctrl+S or :wq in Vim, depending on your editor). Verify: `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows) — you'll see CLAUDE.md in the project folder.
If /init doesn't work — you may have typed it in a regular claude.ai chat, not Claude Code: /init is a Claude Code slash command, make sure you're in the terminal session.
Now think: what real task would you delegate to Claude right now? E.g., "help me structure my notes", "let's analyze this document", "sketch a plan for project X".

Phrase the request in the "Role → Task → Format" style (if you don't remember — do the basics tutorial afterward). Example: "I'm working on <your context>. Help me <specific task> in <markdown / list / table> format. If you need inputs — ask questions."
Send it to Claude Code, read the answer. If Claude wants to create a file — allow it, that's normal in your working folder.
s6.validate: A CLAUDE.md file appeared in the folder with your custom rules; Claude gave a meaningful answer tied to your context, possibly created a file in the project folder.
s6.tip: Don't try to make a perfect CLAUDE.md on the first try — it's a living document. Next learning steps: the basics tutorial — for theory of models and context, the claude-code tutorial — for deeper /security-review, hooks, subagents.

applyIn.title: Before launching Claude Code
applyIn.description: Every session starts with `cd` into the right folder. Without terminal vocabulary — no way.

applyIn.title: Any instruction on the internet
applyIn.description: "Open the terminal and run..." — no longer triggers panic.

applyIn.title: Installing any tool
applyIn.description: npm, brew, pip — all via the terminal. One vocabulary — dozens of tools.

pitfalls: Skipping ahead without running the steps — theory without practice doesn't stick.
Trying to work in /Applications or /System — those need permissions. Use home (~/).
Ignoring errors — the terminal always tells you what went wrong. Read and fix.

exercises.question: After finishing — open the terminal again, navigate to ~/projects/ and run pwd + ls. From memory only.
exercises.hint: If you forgot a command — look back at the steps. Remembering is fine.

exercises.question: Create a nested structure: ~/projects/test/2026/january/. Use a single mkdir -p.

s1.title: pwd — find out where you are now
s1.why: The terminal is always "inside" some folder. Finding out which is the first command of the day.
instructions: Open the terminal (if it isn't already): macOS Cmd+Space → "Terminal"; Windows — PowerShell.
Type: `pwd` (mac/linux/PowerShell) → press Enter.
Look at the output. That's the path to the folder you're in right now.
s1.example:
Mac: /Users/denisa
Windows: C:\Users\denisa
Usually when the terminal starts you're in your home — that's normal.
s1.validate: You see a line like /Users/<name> (mac) or C:\Users\<name> (Windows).
s1.tip: pwd = "print working directory". The simpler the command, the more often you use it. This one — literally every time.

s2.title: ls / dir — look at what's around
s2.why: Without ls you're flying blind. ls shows what folders and files are in the current one.
instructions: macOS / Linux: type `ls` → Enter.
Windows (PowerShell): `ls` works too. Old cmd.exe — `dir`.
Look at the list. That's the contents of your home folder: Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.
s2.example:
Mac/Linux output:
Applications  Desktop  Documents  Downloads  Movies  Music  Pictures  projects  Public

Windows output (dir):
  <DIR>  Documents
  <DIR>  Downloads
  ...
s2.validate: You see a list of folders: at least Desktop, Documents, Downloads.
s2.tip: `ls -la` (mac) shows hidden files (starting with .) and details. Useful later when you're looking for the .claude/ folder.

s3.title: mkdir + cd — create a folder and enter it
s3.why: That's the entire "start a new project" toolkit: create a folder → enter it.
instructions: Create a test folder: `mkdir tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
Check it appeared: `ls` → it should be in the list.
Enter it: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
Verify you're inside: `pwd` → should end with /tutorial-sandbox.
s3.validate: pwd prints a path ending with /tutorial-sandbox. Folder created, you're in it.
s3.tip: Tab is your best friend. Start typing `cd tut` → press Tab → the terminal completes to `cd tutorial-sandbox/`. Saves 90% of typing.

s4.title: cd .. and cd ~ — navigate back
s4.why: Knowing how to go back is as important as going in. Insurance against "where did I end up?".
instructions: You're now in tutorial-sandbox. Type `cd ..` → Enter. (Two dots = "folder above".)
Check: `pwd` → you're back in home.
Now go back in: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → verify pwd.
From anywhere you can return home with one command: `cd ~` (or just `cd`).
s4.validate: You understand: `..` = up one level, `~` = home, any path = a specific place.
s4.tip: On Windows the tilde (~) also works in PowerShell. `cd` with no arguments always returns home.

s5.title: Lock it in — a nested structure in one command
s5.why: Real task: create ~/projects/<name>/notes/ in one go. `mkdir -p` can do it.
instructions: From anywhere type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-project/notes` → Enter.
Enter it: `cd ~/projects/my-first-project` → check `ls` (you should see the notes folder).
You can delete the test: `cd ~` → then `rm -r tutorial-sandbox` (Mac/Linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse tutorial-sandbox` (PowerShell). This removes the folder permanently.
Don't delete ~/projects/my-first-project — it'll come in handy in the first-project tutorial.
s5.validate: You see the notes folder inside ~/projects/my-first-project. Structure created in one command.
s5.tip: -p (parents) is a super useful flag. Without it, mkdir fails if the parent folder doesn't exist. With it — creates the whole chain.

troubleshoot.rm doesn't work on Windows: Windows uses `del` or `rmdir /s`. PowerShell handles `Remove-Item -Recurse`. When in doubt — delete via Explorer.
troubleshoot.Tab completion doesn't work: Normal for cmd.exe. Switch to PowerShell or Windows Terminal — autocomplete works there.

s6.title: Ctrl+C and clear — safely cancel and tidy up
s6.why: Sooner or later a command will "hang" or you'll change your mind halfway. Knowing how to stop it is peace of mind: you can always hit "cancel" without breaking anything.
instructions: Run an "endless" command so there's something to interrupt: `ping example.com` (Mac/Linux) — lines will scroll forever.
Press `Ctrl+C` — the command stops and you get the prompt back. It's safe: Ctrl+C just interrupts the current command, it doesn't touch your files.
If you've half-typed a line and changed your mind — press `Ctrl+C` again: the terminal clears the line so you can start over.
When the screen is cluttered with output — type `clear` (Mac/Linux/PowerShell) → Enter. The screen clears, but your command history stays (the up arrow brings back past commands).
s6.example:
$ ping example.com
PING example.com ...
64 bytes from ...
^C        ← here you pressed Ctrl+C
$         ← prompt is back, everything under control
s6.validate: After Ctrl+C the command stopped and the prompt ($ or >) returned. After `clear` the screen is clean, and the up arrow still shows past commands.
s6.tip: `Ctrl+C` means "interrupt", not "copy" (a habit from other apps). To confirm a command finished rather than hung — watch the prompt: `$` / `>` is back = the command is done.

troubleshoot.Ctrl+C does nothing: Sometimes you need to press it twice. If it's really stuck — close the terminal tab and open a new one: no files are harmed by this.
troubleshoot.clear made my command history disappear: It didn't. `clear` only wipes the visible screen. Press the up arrow — your past commands are still there.

folders-workshop.title: Folders workshop: 3 structure examples
folders-workshop.subtitle: Audits, notes, experiment — build structure for three real cases
folders-workshop.whatItIs: Want to create folders with clicks in Finder/Explorer, or with a command in the terminal — your choice. This tutorial shows both ways across three live scenarios: work reports, personal notes, a throwaway experiment.
folders-workshop.approach: Don't pick ONE way. Create every folder both ways — via Finder AND via mkdir. After 3 rounds, your preference becomes deliberate.
outcomes: Create folders via both UI and terminal
Know which names won't cause problems
Understand how to organize the project tree meaningfully
Can cleanly delete temporary experiments

applyIn.title: Every new project
applyIn.description: First step — a folder with a meaningful name in ~/projects/. Otherwise — chaos in a month.

applyIn.title: Personal knowledge base
applyIn.description: A separate hierarchy for notes, learning, recipes — kept apart from work folders.

applyIn.title: Experiment / sandbox
applyIn.description: A "trash" folder you're not afraid to delete. Every professional has one.

pitfalls: Spaces and non-ASCII in names — the terminal and git don't like them. "my project" ❌ → "my-project" ✅.
Folders on the Desktop — a week later there are 30 of them and you can't find anything. Use ~/projects/.
Deleting a folder with rm -rf without checking — it's gone forever. ls first, then rm.

exercises.question: Create your own ~/projects/ structure: at least 3 projects with meaningful names. One via Finder, two via mkdir.
exercises.hint: Names should answer "what is this?" 6 months later. "test" — bad. "monthly-reports-2026" — good.

exercises.question: Delete a temp folder both ways: once via the Trash (drag-to-trash), once via rm -r. Notice the difference.
exercises.hint: Trash → recoverable. rm -r → no, gone forever. When in doubt — Trash.

s1.title: Decide on a name and structure (naming rules)
s1.why: A folder name is a future `cd <this name>` command. Long / spaces / non-ASCII — you'll suffer every time.
instructions: Rule 1: ASCII only. No non-Latin letters.
Rule 2: instead of spaces — hyphens (or underscores). work-reports, not work reports.
Rule 3: the name answers "what's inside?" (≤ 30 chars). monthly-audits is better than stuff.
Rule 4: one folder — one topic. Don't dump different things into one.
s1.example:
Good: monthly-audits, claude-notes, sandbox-2026, website-redesign
Bad: "My projects", stuff, test, untitled folder, new folder (1)
s1.validate: You can explain to yourself: "This folder is about X, the name is short and clear."
s1.tip: If you plan to make a git repo from the folder — pick the name now. Renaming later is possible but noisy.

s2.title: Example 1 — Work audits (via the terminal)
s2.why: Scenario: you plan to do regular audits once a month. You need a shared folder for them.
instructions: Open the terminal.
Type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`. This creates both monthly-audits and the May subfolder.
Enter it: `cd ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`.
Verify: `pwd` — ends with /monthly-audits/2026-may. Structure is ready to use.
s2.validate: You see the full path to 2026-may. Folder created, you're in it.
s2.tip: Subfolders by date (2026-may) follow the "new month = new folder" pattern. Scales very robustly.

s3.title: Example 2 — Notes and learning (via Finder/Explorer)
s3.why: Scenario: you're learning something new and want to keep notes. Visual is more convenient — that's fine.
instructions: macOS: open Finder → Cmd+Shift+H (return to home) → find the projects folder (or create it with Cmd+Shift+N).
Inside projects: right click → New Folder → type `learning-notes` → Enter.
Inside learning-notes — create two more: `claude` and `terminal-basics`.
Windows: open Explorer → navigate to C:\Users\<name>\projects → right click → New Folder. Repeat for subfolders.
s3.example:
The Finder structure:
projects/
  learning-notes/
    claude/
    terminal-basics/
s3.validate: In Finder/Explorer you see the tree: projects → learning-notes → claude / terminal-basics.
s3.tip: Terminal and Finder work on the same filesystem. A folder created in one is visible in the other. You can mix them.

s4.title: Example 3 — Temporary experiment (any method)
s4.why: Scenario: you want to experiment with something — you need a single-use folder you won't regret deleting.
instructions: Create it however you like: `mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox` (terminal) OR via Finder.
Create some folders and files inside — anything. For example: `cd ~/projects/sandbox && touch test.txt && mkdir notes`.
Check the contents: `ls` — should show test.txt and notes.
Remember: this folder is a deletion candidate in step 5.
s4.prompt:
mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox
cd ~/projects/sandbox
touch test.txt
mkdir notes
ls
s4.validate: In sandbox you see test.txt and notes/. Folder filled and ready for deletion.
s4.tip: touch creates an empty file in a second. Handy for quick tests. Windows equivalent: `New-Item test.txt` or `echo. > test.txt`.

s5.title: Clean deletion — two ways
s5.why: Learning to delete is as important as learning to create. Otherwise folders pile up endlessly.
instructions: Way 1 (safe) — via Finder/Explorer: open ~/projects/, drag sandbox to the Trash. Can be undone if you change your mind.
Way 2 (fast, irreversible) — `rm -rf ~/projects/sandbox` (mac/linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force ~/projects/sandbox` (PowerShell).
IMPORTANT: rm -rf deletes INSTANTLY, no Trash. Double-check the path before Enter.
Verify it's gone: `ls ~/projects/` — sandbox is no longer in the list.
s5.example:
Before: $ ls ~/projects/
monthly-audits  learning-notes  sandbox  my-first-project

After:
monthly-audits  learning-notes  my-first-project
s5.validate: ~/projects/ no longer contains sandbox. Experiment closed, working folders intact.
s5.tip: Never type rm -rf / or rm -rf ~/ — it deletes EVERYTHING. Always specify a concrete path and read it twice.

troubleshoot.rm: command not found on Windows: Use PowerShell with `Remove-Item -Recurse` or just Explorer + Delete.
troubleshoot.Trash doesn't restore on mac: Cmd+Shift+Delete empties the Trash. If you already emptied — files are lost (only Time Machine can recover, if enabled).

s6.title: Protect an important folder: your first backup with git
s6.why: Work folders (like monthly-audits) hurt to lose. Set up git once and you get version history and a safety net: even if you delete a file by accident, you can bring it back.
instructions: Go into the folder you want to protect: `cd ~/projects/monthly-audits`.
Create a repository: `git init`. This turns on change tracking inside the folder.
Save the first snapshot: `git add .` then `git commit -m "initial backup"`.
Confirm the snapshot is saved: `git log --oneline` — you'll see your "initial backup" commit.
s6.prompt:
cd ~/projects/monthly-audits
git init
git add .
git commit -m "initial backup"
git log --oneline
s6.validate: git log shows the "initial backup" commit. Your folder now has a restore point.
s6.tip: Run a new `git commit` after every meaningful change — it's like "saving the game": you can always return to a working version. If git isn't installed — on mac run `xcode-select --install`.
